11.t: Working with data: a knockout study
q: Calculate the percentage increase in mass of the knockout mice.
Use the food data to explain why the knockout mice become obese.
Without leptin the brain never receives the "enough fat stored" signal, so the mice eat almost twice as much food.
Explain why the injected group strengthens the conclusion that leptin controls body mass.
Giving back only the missing protein restores normal mass and appetite, so the obesity was caused by the lack of leptin, not by another effect of the knockout process.
Suggest why most obese people do not benefit from leptin injections.
Most obese people already have high leptin; their brain cells do not respond to it (leptin resistance), so adding more has little effect.
State one ethical issue with knockout studies like this.
Animals may suffer (obesity, poor health); numbers used should be kept to a minimum.

17.t: Working with data: a conserved protein
q: Calculate the percentage of human cytochrome c amino acids that differ in yeast.
Explain why cytochrome c can be compared across such different organisms.
All eukaryotes respire aerobically and need it in the electron transport chain, so every species has a version of the same protein.
Explain why the number of differences rises with evolutionary distance.
Mutations accumulate at a roughly steady rate after two lineages separate, so species with a more distant common ancestor differ more.
Yeast cytochrome c still works in human mitochondria. Explain how this is possible with 45 differences.
Most differences are in less important positions; the amino acids of the active and binding sites are conserved, so the shape and function are kept.
Suggest why cytochrome c changes so slowly compared with most proteins.
Almost any change to it is harmful (respiration fails), so most mutations are removed by natural selection: it is highly conserved.
